what_it_does: Large language models generate text one word (token) at a time, and each step requires reading the entire set of model weights from memory — this makes memory bandwidth (how fast data can travel between memory and the processor) the primary bottleneck, not raw computation speed. Standard two-dimensional memory chips sitting beside a processor chip cannot supply data fast enough, so this paper proposes physically stacking 3D memory chips directly on top of the logic chip, dramatically shortening the data path and multiplying available bandwidth. On top of that, the design embeds small compute units inside the memory itself (called compute-in-memory, or CiM — doing math where the data lives rather than moving it out), using a dataflow strategy that keeps each generated token's data resident in place (token-stationary) to minimize unnecessary data movement. An architectural search then allocates the compute-in-memory resources to maximize how many tokens can be generated in parallel. Exact throughput and power numbers should be verified in the full paper.
